title: Executive Roles and Reporting Lines

know: What the CTO, CPO, VP Engineering and the heads of design, data and security are each for.
The common configurations — CTO and CPO as peers, a combined CPTO, CTO with a VP Engineering — and what each trades.

The 'first team' principle as Larson applies it to engineering executives (the term is usually credited to Lencioni; the attribution is not confirmed in the author's notes), and Larson's advice on working with the CEO and peers.
believe: An executive's first team is the executive team, not the function they lead.
can_do: Choose a configuration for a company's stage and constraints.
Decide where design, data and security report and say what the choice costs.
Recognize a structure built around a person and not a decision.

audience.who: Executives (CEO, CTO, CPO, VP, Director) who design or sit in the top of a product and tech organization, and individual contributors who want to follow the reasoning.
already_knows: How software teams work day to day; what product managers, engineering managers and designers do.

From earlier chapters: judgment as a scarce capacity (chapter 5), Corvane's stages and incidents (preface), outcomes and the roadmap's three shares (chapters 9 and 11), the engineering strategy (chapter 13).
does_not_know: CPO, CTO, VP Engineering as accountabilities

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a company described by stage and people, the reader recommends a configuration and names what it gives up.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A 150-person company has a founder CTO who is strong technically and weak on people management, no head of product, and product decisions made by the CEO. Using only this chapter: what leadership configuration would you propose, and what does it give up?
acceptance_criteria.expected: For example a VP Engineering under or beside the CTO to run the organization, and a head of product or CPO to take product decisions off the CEO; it gives up single-point joining of product and technology, which must then be made explicit between the roles.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter gives data, design and security leadership one section each and says where the author's sources are thin.
Concepts taken from a named source name the book and the concept; rules of thumb are presented as that author's rule of thumb; anything applied beyond the source is marked as the author's extension.
Each pattern in the chapter names its user and an outcome measure by which a reader could tell that it worked.

thesis.question: Which executive roles does a product and tech organization need, and who should report to whom?
thesis.claim: A product and tech organization needs, at the top, someone accountable for what is built, someone accountable for how it is built and run, and a place where those two are joined; as peers, a CTO and a CPO, where the balance between the two matters more than speed, or as one combined executive where speed matters more than balance; and, with either, a VP Engineering beside the CTO where the hardest joining is between technical direction and running the engineering organization; and design, data and security should report where their decisions most often need to be joined with others.
thesis.disputed_by: The practice of shaping executive roles around the strengths and ambitions of the people in them, on the grounds that the right people matter more than the chart.
thesis.so_what: A leader designing the top of the organization starts from the decisions that must be made jointly, and treats a role created to retain someone as a cost to be stated.
thesis.how_why: At the top, the scarce capacity is judgment across functions. Two peers join product and engineering by negotiation, which is slow but balanced; one combined executive joins them in one head, which is fast and lopsided; each configuration moves the difficulty and none removes it. The first-team principle, which Larson applies to engineering executives and which is usually credited to Lencioni (the author's notes on neither book show the attribution, so the chapter hedges it), is what makes peers work: each puts the company's outcome before the function's.

supporting_claims.claim: At the top, what is built and how it is built and run are two accountabilities whose decisions meet, and a top that does not say where they are joined leaves the join to be discovered below.

Each of the three common configurations puts that join in a different place and trades one kind of joining for another: peers join by negotiation, which is balanced and slow; one combined executive joins in one head, which is fast and lopsided; a CTO with a VP Engineering adds a join inside engineering.
The configuration is chosen from the hardest join the company has at its stage, and a role shaped around a person is a cost to be stated.
Peers work only when each treats the executive team as the first team, and the practice that makes this concrete is a written list of the decisions they make together and a joint way to escalate.
Design, data and security report where their decisions most often need to be joined with others, and each choice has a cost that can be named.
AI adds decisions that need joining at the top across product, engineering and security, and the same rule decides whether a new role is warranted.

role.contribution: Sets the top of the structure and the principle — roles follow decisions that must be joined — that the rest of the part applies.

additional_patterns.applies_to: what-the-top-must-hold through first-team: the accountabilities and the join before the configurations that place the join, the configurations before the way to choose one, the choice before the practice that makes a join between peers hold.

where-design-reports, where-data-reports, where-security-reports: three applications of one rule, stated once at the start of the first. Design comes first because its decisions meet product decisions most directly; data second because its jobs divide between product and engineering; security last because its head must sometimes disagree with the executive it reports to, and because the AI section that follows needs security.

flow.rationale: The reader first meets two executives who cannot agree who leads eleven teams, so the model arrives as the missing thing. The accountabilities and the join must be defined before the configurations, which are arrangements of them; the choice among configurations needs all three described; the first-team practice comes after the choice because it is what a join between two people needs, and because Corvane's 2025 page, which resolves the opening scene, is the last stage of the history that the first pattern's table tells; put before the choice, the page would arrive before the reader knows how Corvane came to have two peers. Design, data and security come after both patterns because they apply the same rule to smaller cases; put earlier they would stand between the scene's question and its answer. AI comes last because it adds decisions to a structure the reader must already have.

hook.content: When Corvane appointed its first CPO in 2025, the CTO and the CPO each drew the organization they needed. The two drawings showed the same teams, and for eleven of them they named a different leader.

bridge.from_reader_world: A reader who has seen executive roles settled by who was available and who had to be kept, and a reorganization argued as a contest of charts.
bridge.to_topic: The question a chart cannot answer: which decisions must be made together at the top, and where.

thesis_statement.text: A product and tech organization needs, at the top, someone accountable for what is built, someone accountable for how it is built and run, and a place where those two are joined; as peers, a CTO and a CPO, where the balance between the two matters more than speed; as one combined executive where speed matters more than balance; and as a CTO with a VP Engineering where the hardest joining is between technical direction and running the engineering organization; and design, data and security should report where their decisions most often need to be joined with others.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

promises.promise: See two executives draw one organization two ways at Corvane.
Know what the top must hold and what each executive role is for.
Know the three common configurations and what each trades.
Choose a configuration from the hardest join, and make a join between peers hold with the first-team principle.
Decide where design, data and security report, and know where the author's sources are thin.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2025 Corvane's CTO and its newly appointed CPO each drew the organization they needed, and the two drawings named a different leader for eleven teams.

evidence.what: Illustration: Corvane, 2025, growing toward 500 people; Tomas Rell (co-founder and CTO), Priya Nambiar (CPO from 2025), Ines Okafor (co-founder and CEO); the same teams in both drawings, a different leader for eleven of them.
evidence.shows: A top where nobody has said where product and engineering are joined.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional; new facts appended by this chapter)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The top needs someone accountable for what is built, someone accountable for how it is built and run, and a place where the two are joined; three configurations put that place differently and each fits a condition; the chapter goes from the scene through the roles, the configurations, two patterns, three reporting lines and AI.

transition_in.carries_over: Two drawings that could not be reconciled.
transition_in.introduces: What the drawings left out, the chapter's claim, and the route through the chapter.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene: Two Drawings of One Organization
sections.controlling_idea: Corvane's two drawings each followed from what its author was accountable for, and they could not be reconciled by redrawing because the word 'leads' stood for decisions nobody had listed.

advances_thesis.how: Shows a top where two accountabilities meet and nobody has said where they are joined.

transition_in.carries_over: The lead's short account of the two drawings.
transition_in.introduces: What each drawing said and why neither was wrong.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each drawing was reasonable: the CTO's put each of the eleven teams under its engineering manager and the CPO's put it under its product manager, and each followed from what its author was accountable for.

evidence.what: Illustration: 2025, Corvane growing toward 500 people; eleven product teams exist and more are being formed. Tomas Rell's drawing (made with Dario Vance): team -> engineering manager -> engineering director -> VP Engineering -> CTO, with product managers assigned to teams. Priya Nambiar's drawing: team -> product manager -> group product lead -> CPO, with engineers staffed to teams. The teams still to be formed are unnamed boxes in both.
evidence.shows: Each author drew the line along which their own accountability runs.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional; new facts appended by this chapter)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Redrawing could not settle the disagreement, because 'leads' stood for decisions nobody had listed, and the disagreement was already at work inside the teams.

evidence.what: Illustration: in three of the eleven teams the engineering manager and the product manager had each been told by their own executive that they set the team's plan for the next quarter.
evidence.shows: The gap at the top had already become a conflict one level down.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional; new facts appended by this chapter)

transition_in.introduces: Why they disagreed and what the disagreement was already doing.

sections.heading: What the Top of the Organization Must Hold
sections.controlling_idea: The top of a product and tech organization must hold accountability for what is built, accountability for how it is built and run, and a place where the two are joined; executive titles are names for parts of this and must be read by the decisions they make.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the two accountabilities, the join and the roles, which the configurations then arrange.

flow.rationale: The two accountabilities and the join come first, then the titles that carry them, then the warning that a title does not fix the job, which the configurations need.

transition_in.introduces: What the top has to hold, stated as accountabilities and a join.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The top must hold three things: someone accountable for what is built, someone accountable for how it is built and run, and a place where decisions that need both kinds of knowledge are joined.

evidence.what: The author's framing. A joined decision is one that cannot be made well with the knowledge of one side alone; examples: how much capacity goes to new product and how much to keeping the product running; whether a promise to a customer can be kept by its date; which teams exist and what each owns.
evidence.shows: Makes 'joined' concrete with three decisions every such organization meets.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Six executive roles recur, and each is for one part of this: the CPO, the CTO and the VP Engineering for the two accountabilities, and the heads of design, data and security for decisions that cut across them.

evidence.what: Role | Is for | A decision it makes. CPO (chief product officer) | what is built: whose problem, which problem, in what order | which outcome a product group works on this year. CTO (chief technology officer) | how it is built and run: technical direction, and often the engineering organization | which technical choices are made once for all teams. VP Engineering | running the engineering organization: managers, hiring, delivery | how many engineers each group gets. Head of design | whether people can use what is built | the standard a screen must meet before release. Head of data | the data the company decides with and builds on | what a metric means across teams. Head of security | stating risk and the controls against it | which risks are brought to the CEO to accept.
evidence.shows: One line per role, so that the configurations can be read as arrangements of these.

evidence.what: Larson defines the Engineering executive as the functional leader for Engineering, responsible for both technical execution and people management within Engineering.
evidence.shows: The source's definition holds two jobs in one role, which the next paragraph separates.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes

transition_in.introduces: The titles that usually carry them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The engineering side holds two jobs, technical direction and running the organization, which can sit in one person or in two, so the same title means different things in different companies and a role is read by its decisions.

evidence.what: A CTO in one company runs the whole engineering organization; in another the CTO sets technical direction and a VP Engineering runs the organization; the title alone does not say which.
evidence.shows: Prepares the third configuration and the habit of reading roles by decisions.

transition_in.carries_over: Roles as fixed lines in a table.
transition_in.introduces: The same title covering different jobs.

sections.heading: Three Configurations and What Each Trades
sections.controlling_idea: Three common configurations put the join of product and engineering in three different places, and each trades one kind of joining for another; none removes the difficulty.

advances_thesis.how: Describes each configuration by where the join sits and what it costs, and states the author's mapping of configurations to conditions.

flow.rationale: The figure shows all three first so that each description can point at a place on it; peers and the combined executive are opposites and come as a pair; the CTO with a VP Engineering comes third because it is a division inside the engineering side of either; the table of conditions needs all three.

transition_in.carries_over: The accountabilities, the join and the roles.
transition_in.introduces: The common ways of arranging them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three configurations are common: the first two are alternatives that join product and engineering between two peers or inside one executive, and the third is a division of the engineering side that adds a second join and combines with either of the first two.

evidence.what: Mermaid flowchart with three small org diagrams side by side. Peers: CEO -> CPO, CEO -> CTO, and a labeled link between CPO and CTO ('joined by agreement'). Combined: CEO -> CPTO ('joined in one head') -> Head of Product, Head of Engineering. CTO with VP Engineering: CEO -> CTO -> VP Engineering, with the link between CTO and VP Engineering labeled ('direction joined with running'), and a product executive beside the CTO.
evidence.shows: Shows the join as a place on each chart.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: As peers, a CTO and a CPO join product and engineering by negotiation, which keeps both accountabilities at full strength and costs time, and it needs the CEO as the place a disagreement goes.

evidence.what: Neither peer can overrule the other, so each joined decision is argued by someone accountable for each side; the cost is the time of the argument and a CEO who must decide when the two cannot.
evidence.shows: Names what the peer configuration gives and what it gives up.

transition_in.introduces: What peers give and what they cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: One combined executive joins product and engineering in one head, which is fast, and is lopsided toward the discipline that executive came from, and it becomes a queue as the company grows.

evidence.what: Illustration: Corvane in 2019, 12 people: Tomas Rell decided product and technology alone; decisions were quick and consistent until every pricing, design and release decision waited for him (the Founder Queue).
evidence.shows: The combined configuration at its best and at its limit.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional; new facts appended by this chapter)

transition_in.introduces: Joining in one person.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A CTO with a VP Engineering splits the engineering side into technical direction and running the organization, which gives each a full-time owner and creates a new join between them, and it leaves the join with product where it was.

evidence.what: A decision such as whether to pause feature work for a migration needs both the direction and the organization's capacity; with two people it has to be agreed between them.
evidence.shows: Shows that the third configuration adds a join and does not remove one.

transition_in.introduces: Two people dividing the engineering side.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Which configuration fits depends on which joining is hardest for the company: peers where balance matters more than speed, one combined executive where speed matters more, a CTO with a VP Engineering where the hardest joining is between technical direction and running the organization. This mapping is the author's position.

evidence.what: Configuration | Where product and engineering are joined | Fits when | Gives up. CTO and CPO as peers | between the two, by agreement, with the CEO behind | balance matters more than speed: a mistake toward either side is expensive | speed; a single point of joining. One combined executive | in one head | speed matters more than balance: small company, or one product in fast change | balance; the executive's time as the company grows. CTO with a VP Engineering | wherever it was before (with a product peer, or in the CTO) | the hardest joining is between technical direction and running the organization | a single voice for engineering; the new join must be written.
evidence.shows: States the author's mapping in one place, with what each gives up.

transition_in.carries_over: Three configurations described one by one.
transition_in.introduces: The conditions under which each fits, as the author's position.

sections.heading: Pattern: Choose the Configuration from the Hardest Join
sections.controlling_idea: The configuration is chosen by finding the joined decisions that waited or went wrong and putting a person or a written agreement on the hardest of them; Corvane's four stages show each choice answering one join and creating the next, and a role made for a person is a cost to state.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the mapping into a procedure with a user and an outcome measure, shows it on Corvane, and answers the view that roles should follow people.

flow.rationale: The procedure is stated first, Corvane's history is shown as a table before it is interpreted, the interpretation follows, and the objection comes last because it is answered with the case just read.

transition_in.introduces: How to find which condition a company is in.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The user of this pattern is whoever designs the top (a CEO, founders or a board), and the procedure is to list the joined decisions of the last two quarters, mark where each waited or was made by one side alone, find the hardest join, and choose the configuration for it: a CTO with a VP Engineering when the hardest join is inside engineering, and, when it is product with engineering, peers or one combined executive by the balance-against-speed condition of the mapping table; it worked if joined decisions are made faster and fewer are made twice.

evidence.what: Steps: list the decisions that needed both kinds of knowledge; for each, who made it, how long it waited, whether it was reopened; group them by what had to meet (product with engineering, or technical direction with running the organization); the group with the longest waits and most reversals is the hardest join; choose the configuration for that join, using the mapping table's condition (balance or speed) to decide between peers and one combined executive. Outcome measure: time from raising a joined decision to making it, and the count of such decisions reopened or made by one side alone.
evidence.shows: Gives the reader a way to choose that starts from decisions and can be checked.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Corvane's top went through all three configurations between 2019 and 2025, each at a different size.

evidence.what: Illustration. Years and size | Configuration | Hardest join at the time | What happened. 2019, 12 people | one combined executive in practice: Tomas Rell decides product and technology | none yet, then everything | the Founder Queue. 2020-2022, 50 people | still combined: the first product manager, Priya Nambiar, and later product managers report to Tomas Rell | product with engineering, inside one busy head | the Two Calendars; from 2022 Priya Nambiar decides scheduling rules. 2023-2024, 180 people | CTO with a VP Engineering: Dario Vance runs the organization, Tomas Rell keeps technical direction; eleven product managers still report to the CTO | technical direction with running a hiring wave | the join inside engineering is covered; product has no executive and the roadmap fills with forty-one promised features. 2025-2026, 500 people | CTO and CPO as peers, with the VP Engineering under the CTO | product with engineering, now between two people | the two drawings.
evidence.shows: Each row is one configuration at one size with its result.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional; new facts appended by this chapter)

transition_in.introduces: One company's four answers over seven years.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The table shows each change answering the hardest join of its time and exposing the next, and one change that came late: product stayed under a CTO whose attention was on technology until 2025.

evidence.what: The author's record of Build What Matters: the first product hire is a senior product manager, and a product executive follows when there are several product managers and a founder ready to hand over strategy.
evidence.shows: A source's rule of thumb for when the product side needs its own executive; Corvane had eleven product managers and none.
evidence.source: Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020), through the author's record right-team in grounded-product-management

evidence.what: Illustration: 2024, eleven product managers reporting to the CTO, roadmap rows added by sales (the forty-one features).
evidence.shows: The lopsidedness of the combined configuration at 180 people.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional; new facts appended by this chapter)

transition_in.introduces: What the sequence shows.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The opposing practice shapes roles around the people available; people do constrain the choice, but a role made to keep or fit a person adds a join that someone must carry, so it is stated as a cost, and it can be recognized by asking what decisions the role joins once the name is removed.

evidence.what: Illustration: after 2023 Tomas Rell's role was that of a founder who kept his title while Dario Vance ran engineering; the split between them was not written until 2025, when it was stated as: Tomas Rell holds the technical side of company-level decisions (build or buy, acquisitions, the technology in the company strategy) and is consulted on the engineering strategy; Dario Vance holds everything inside engineering.
evidence.shows: A role built partly around a person, made workable by stating the decisions it holds.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional; new facts appended by this chapter)

evidence.what: Build What Matters names the founder or CEO who cannot let go of product decisions the Throne Room, and says that at a certain point instinct does not scale.
evidence.shows: A source's name for the commonest role built around a person.
evidence.source: Ben Foster and Rajesh Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020); author's Kindle notes

transition_in.introduces: The view that roles should follow the people, and the answer to it.

sections.heading: Pattern: Make the Executive Team the First Team
sections.controlling_idea: Peer executives work when each puts the executive team before the function they lead, and the practice that makes this concrete is a written list of the decisions they make together and an agreed way to escalate jointly; Corvane's 2025 page shows it.

advances_thesis.how: States the first-team principle with its attribution, gives the practice with user and measure, and resolves the two drawings with it.

flow.rationale: The principle and its attribution come first, then why peers need it, then the practice, then Corvane's page as a table before the paragraph that says what it changed; the scene's question is answered here because the answer is the practice.

transition_in.carries_over: A configuration chosen, with joins between people.
transition_in.introduces: What makes a join between peers hold.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An executive's first team is the executive team and not the function they lead; the phrase is usually credited to Lencioni, whose Five Dysfunctions holds the idea as attention to collective results over one's department, and Larson uses the phrase for managers' peers and for the engineering leadership team.

evidence.what: Five Dysfunctions, fifth dysfunction (inattention to results): team members put their individual needs or even the needs of their departments above the collective goals of the team. The author's notes on Lencioni's two books do not contain the phrase 'first team'.
evidence.shows: Where the idea sits in Lencioni as the author's notes have it.
evidence.source: Patrick Lencioni, The Five Dysfunctions of a Team (2002); author's Kindle notes

evidence.what: An Elegant Puzzle: 'make your peers your first team', addressed to managers. The Engineering Executive's Primer: the weekly engineering leadership meeting is the forum for forging direct reports into a 'first team' whose top priority is to support each other.
evidence.shows: How Larson uses the phrase, which is for peers at any level and for the executive's own reports.
evidence.source: Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle (2019) and The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes

evidence.what: Applying it to the CTO and CPO as members of the CEO's team is the plain reading of Lencioni and the author's extension of Larson's wording.
evidence.shows: Marks what is the author's extension.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Peers need the principle because an executive who puts the function first turns every joined decision into a contest, and the gap between two executives grows as it travels down.

evidence.what: Larson: when executives are focused on their function rather than the executive team's shared success, allocating expenses is a zero-sum game.
evidence.shows: The cost at the top.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes

evidence.what: 'Like a vortex, small gaps between executives high up in an organization become major discrepancies by the time they reach employees below.'
evidence.shows: Lencioni's account of what Corvane's eleven teams experienced.
evidence.source: Patrick Lencioni, The Five Dysfunctions of a Team (2002); author's Kindle notes

transition_in.introduces: Why a join between peers fails without it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The practice for two peer executives starts from two pieces of Larson's advice: each writes down alone what they expect of the other's role and the two compare, and they agree to escalate jointly (structured escalation); turning the differences into a list of decisions made together is the author's extension. The users are the two peers, and it worked if disagreements reach the CEO from both at once and settled decisions stay settled.

evidence.what: Larson on onboarding a peer executive: your job as a peer executive is to help the new executive succeed; the author's record of the chapter: independently write down expectations of each other's roles and compare them. Larson on structured escalation, a process he attributes to LinkedIn: agree to resolve a disagreement within five days; if you cannot, escalate together with a shared document and commit to the answer.
evidence.shows: Two practices from the source that turn the principle into something two people do.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes and the author's records onboarding-peer-executives and working-with-your-ceo-peers-and-engineering

transition_in.introduces: What two peers do about it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2025 Corvane's CEO asked the CTO and the CPO for a list of decisions in place of a third drawing, and the list they wrote fits on one page.

evidence.what: Illustration: Corvane's 2025 page. Decision | Who decides | Who must be heard first. Which outcomes each product group works on, and their order | CPO | CTO and VP Engineering, on what each would cost. How it is built, the technical standards, who is hired and how engineers are managed | VP Engineering, within the CTO's technical direction | CPO, on what the product needs next. The share of capacity for innovation, iteration and operation | CPO and CTO together | the group directors. Which teams exist, what each owns, and who leads each product group | CPO and CTO together | VP Engineering and the people affected. What a team does this quarter | the team's product manager and engineering manager together, within the outcome it was given | the designer. A disagreement between the two executives | both go to the CEO within five working days with one page | none.
evidence.shows: The drawings' question, who leads a team, replaced by who decides what.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional; new facts appended by this chapter)

transition_in.introduces: The practice at Corvane.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The page settled what the drawings could not, since each of the eleven teams kept both an engineering manager and a product manager and the two now had a named shared decision, and it had a visible cost in the time the joint decisions took.

evidence.what: Illustration: in the quarter before the page nine disagreements between product and engineering reached Ines Okafor, each brought by one side; in the two quarters after it four did, each brought by both with one page. The chart that followed kept two lines (engineering managers to group directors to the VP Engineering; product managers to the CPO). The capacity share (40/35/25) was the first decision made under the joint row. The cost: in 2026 quarterly planning took nine of thirteen weeks (the Nine-Week Plan), which this chapter reads in part as the price of joining by agreement.
evidence.shows: Result and cost of the peer configuration with a written join.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional; new facts appended by this chapter)

transition_in.introduces: What it changed and what it cost.

sections.heading: Where Design Reports
sections.controlling_idea: Design reports where its decisions most often need joining, which is usually with product, and each line has a cost; the author's sources say little about the design executive.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the chapter's rule to the first of three functions and says how far the sources go.

transition_in.carries_over: The rule that a role sits where its decisions are joined, applied to the CTO and CPO.
transition_in.introduces: The same rule applied to design, then data and security.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The rule that placed the CTO and the CPO places the other heads too: a function reports where its decisions most often need to be joined with others. A head of design, accountable for whether people can use what is built, reports either to the CPO, where design decisions meet product decisions daily, or to the CEO as a third peer, where design has its own voice and adds a party to every joined decision.

evidence.what: The author's judgment. Under the CPO: discovery and roadmap decisions are joined with design in one line; the cost is that design can come to serve the roadmap. As a peer: usability has a voice equal to value and feasibility; the cost is three-way negotiation at the top. The rule: put the line where most of design's decisions need joining, and name what the other line would have given.
evidence.shows: Options with costs, as the thesis requires.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's sources are thin on the design executive: Build What Matters, as the author's record of it has it, says only that design should be a function of its own that works with product as a peer and that designers should not report to individual product managers; a book on the subject exists and is not on the author's bookshelf.

evidence.what: The author's record right-team (after Build What Matters): separate design from product management as soon as the company can afford it; avoid designers reporting into individual product managers once the design team grows; product and design are peers.
evidence.shows: What the author's sources do say.

sections.heading: Where Data Reports
sections.controlling_idea: Data leadership holds three different jobs that join with different parts of the organization, so it reports where the job that matters most is joined; the author's sources say almost nothing about it.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the rule to data and states the gap in the sources.

transition_in.carries_over: Design placed by where its decisions are joined.
transition_in.introduces: Data placed by the same rule.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A head of data may hold three jobs (the data platform, analysis for decisions, and data built into the product) and each joins with a different part of the organization: the platform with engineering, analysis with product and the business, and data in the product with both.

evidence.what: The author's judgment. Under engineering: pipelines and the platform are run like other shared services; cost: analysis becomes a ticket queue for product. Under product: analysts sit with the decisions they inform; cost: the platform is under-engineered. A data executive of its own: only where data is itself what the company sells or where a regulator requires it; cost: one more peer at the top.
evidence.shows: Options with costs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's sources do not treat the data executive at all: Larson's Primer, as the author's record of it has it, names data only as a domain to check for in the engineering leadership team; what this section says is the author's judgment.

evidence.what: The author's record gelling-your-engineering-leadership-team (after Larson's chapter): check whether key domains such as Data, Security and Infrastructure are represented in the leadership team.
evidence.shows: The whole of what the sources offer.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024), through the author's record gelling-your-engineering-leadership-team

evidence.what: Illustration: Corvane in 2026 has no head of data; product analysts report into Priya Nambiar's organization and the data pipelines belong to the platform team under Lena Brandt; the cost is that no one person decides what a measure such as first-visit completion means in both places.

sections.heading: Where Security Reports
sections.controlling_idea: Security reports either inside engineering, close to the systems, or outside it, independent of the deadlines it may slow, and whichever line is chosen it needs a direct path to the CEO; the author's sources say little.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the rule to security and states the gap in the sources.

transition_in.carries_over: Data placed by where its decisions are joined.
transition_in.introduces: Security placed by the same rule, with one difference.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A head of security is accountable for stating risk and for the controls against it, and the reporting line trades closeness to the systems against independence from the executive whose deadlines a control may slow, so either line needs a direct path to the CEO for a risk only the CEO can accept.

evidence.what: The author's judgment. Under the CTO or VP Engineering: security decisions are joined with engineering decisions every day; cost: the head of security reports to the person who may want the risk accepted. To the CEO, a COO or a legal head: independence; cost: distance from the teams, and a function that reviews from outside becomes a queue (the Review Bottleneck).
evidence.shows: Options with costs, and the one feature the author holds necessary in both.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's sources mention security only in passing, as a specialized engineering role, as a concern that belongs to the whole company and as a question to ask about an acquisition; none says where its head should report.

evidence.what: Larson's Primer: security engineering among specialized roles within engineering; security among things that should be fundamental company concerns; 'Who's responsible for security at the company, and what are they doing?' as a due-diligence question.
evidence.shows: The whole of what the sources offer.
evidence.source: Will Larson, The Engineering Executive's Primer (2024); author's Kindle notes

evidence.what: Illustration: at Corvane a security lead has reported to Dario Vance since 2025, with a standing agreement that a risk Dario Vance would accept and the security lead would not goes to Ines Okafor from both.
evidence.shows: The rule applied.

sections.heading: What AI Changes Here
sections.controlling_idea: AI use adds decisions that need product, engineering and security joined at the top, and the chapter's rule, a role for a join and not for a topic, decides whether a new executive role is warranted.

advances_thesis.how: Extends the rule to the decisions AI adds, with labeled claims.

transition_in.carries_over: Six roles placed by the decisions they join.
transition_in.introduces: A new set of decisions that needs joining.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Decisions about AI use (which agents and providers, what data may leave the company, what the product may do with a model) need product, engineering and security together, and where nobody at the top holds that join each team decides for itself.

evidence.what: Emerging: the author's observation as of November 2026, not a measured result. Illustration: Corvane in 2027-2028, fourteen teams each with their own coding agent, model provider and prompt conventions, and security unable to say what data left the company.
evidence.shows: A joined decision nobody held, with its result.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional; new facts appended by this chapter)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Whether AI calls for a new executive role or a different configuration is open: by this chapter's rule a role for AI is warranted only where there is a join no existing role can make, and shorter distance between deciding and building may favor the combined executive.

evidence.what: Speculative. It would be confirmed if companies that appoint a head of AI can name decisions that role joins and others could not, and if the share of companies with one combined product and technology executive rises among companies that build mostly with agents.
evidence.shows: Says what would confirm each half.

transition_in.introduces: What may follow for roles and configurations.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The three configurations are three places to put one join. Corvane used all three and each answered the hardest joining of its size; what failed each time was not the configuration but a join nobody had written down, between Tomas Rell and everyone in 2019, between product and a busy CTO in 2024, between two peers in 2025.
conclusion.so_what: A leader designing the top starts from the decisions that must be made jointly, chooses the configuration that puts a person or a written agreement on the hardest of them, and treats a role created to retain someone as a cost to be stated.

callback.to: The two drawings that disagreed about who led eleven teams.
callback.how: The reader can now say that the drawings answered the wrong question, and what the right question (who decides what, and what is decided together) produced.

takeaway.content: List the decisions of the last two quarters that needed both product and engineering, mark where each waited, and write the short page of who decides what and what is decided together.

open_questions: Attribution of 'first team': the journal spec calls it Lencioni's term. The author's notes on The Five Dysfunctions and The Four Obsessions do not contain the phrase; Larson's essay and notes use it without crediting Lencioni; a web check found only secondary sources crediting Lencioni. The chapter says the phrase is usually credited to Lencioni, gives the idea from his fifth dysfunction, and quotes Larson's own uses. The author may want to confirm the phrase against the primary text of The Five Dysfunctions or The Advantage.

Larson's notes use 'first team' for managers' peers (An Elegant Puzzle) and for the executive's direct reports (the Primer), not for the CEO's team as such; the application to CTO and CPO is marked as the plain reading of Lencioni and the author's extension of Larson.

New Corvane facts invented here and appended to the ledger: product managers reported to Tomas Rell until 2025; Dario Vance reports to Tomas Rell; the 2025 written split between them; the two drawings in detail (engineering manager against product manager as leader of each of the eleven teams); the 2025 one-page list of decisions; nine and four escalations to Ines Okafor; Noor Achterberg reports to Priya Nambiar; no head of data in 2026; a security lead under Dario Vance from 2025. The author should check them against chapters 19 to 22, which are written in parallel or later.
Chapter 13 left Tomas Rell's part in the engineering strategy unstated. This chapter says he is consulted on it and does not write it, and that he holds the technical side of company-level decisions.

The ledger says each product group is 'under a director'; this chapter keeps one director per group in the engineering line and adds that product managers report up to the CPO. Chapter 19 (group-level triad) and chapter 20 (layers) must agree.
The chapter reads the Nine-Week Plan of 2026 in part as the cost of joining by agreement between peers; chapter 23 owns the incident and may read it differently.

The design, data and security sections are the author's judgment almost entirely. Org Design for Design Orgs is cited only through a 2016 O'Reilly interview with Merholz that was fetched and read; the book itself was not read.
No 'Where the Sources Disagree' section: the sources do not disagree on this subject, and the opposing view in the thesis (roles follow people) is answered inside the first pattern.
